checks.title: Gibbs–Duhem · 15–21 min
checks.expected_narration: Now consider a binary liquid at fixed temperature and pressure. The Gibbs-Duhem equation connects changes in its two activity coefficients. If one coefficient changes with composition, the other cannot be chosen independently. Their mole-fraction-weighted logarithmic changes must sum to zero. This is a constraint on a collection of composition-dependent properties, rather than a test of one isolated gamma value. The second equation defines dimensionless excess Gibbs energy by weighting the two log activity coefficients. Under the same fixed conditions, the slope of that excess-energy curve equals the logarithm of gamma one divided by gamma two. That slope relationship will give us a local diagnostic. We can compare the slope inferred from the weighted properties with the log ratio at the same composition. Complete B one on page one. State the fixed conditions and explain the connection in one sentence.

checks.title: The experimental path · 21–27 min
checks.expected_narration: Experimental vapor-liquid data do not always follow a path with both temperature and pressure fixed. In an isothermal experiment, temperature stays constant while the equilibrium pressure generally changes with composition. The more general relationship therefore contains a pressure term involving molar excess volume. Our teaching calculation neglects that contribution. This approximation must accompany the interpretation. In an isobaric experiment, pressure is fixed but temperature changes. The local relationship then needs an excess-enthalpy correction. For real measurements, we need independent excess-enthalpy information before assigning that corrected local verdict. A missing correction is not evidence that the measurements failed. Lab Three also supplies synthetic excess enthalpy for its generated isobaric cases. That value comes from the generator; it is not an independent calorimetric measurement. Complete B two: identify the omitted pressure contribution and the property needed for the temperature correction.

checks.title: Area solution · 43–50 min
checks.expected_narration: The four baseline contributions are zero point three seven five, zero point one two five, minus zero point one two five, and minus zero point three seven five. The positive area is one half, the signed negative area is minus one half, and the total is zero. Raising the entire curve by zero point two adds a rectangle of height zero point two over a composition interval of one. The new signed integral is therefore zero point two. Lab Three calls the signed integral I and also reports a normalized score, D. D compares the magnitudes of the positive and negative areas; it is not the signed integral itself. The teaching area criterion is D below five percent. If both magnitudes vanish, that normalization is undefined. Check your work and keep the distinction visible. Real interior measurements still cannot establish missing endpoint intervals without an extra assumption.

checks.title: Model reproduction · 74–80 min
checks.expected_narration: For the one required modeling run, return to Consistent reference at three hundred fifty kelvin and forty-one points. Click Run modeling test once and wait for the convergence message. Then inspect Modeling residuals. Record the pressure error in percent and the vapor-composition error in percentage points. These are different quantities, even though both are scaled by one hundred. The Lab fits two constant N R T L parameters with the nonrandomness parameter fixed at zero point four seven. Its teaching criteria require both reported errors to be below one in their stated units. The clean fit should give near-zero errors because it reproduces its own generating model; that is a check of model reproduction, not a certificate for real measurements. Herington is not applicable because this case is isothermal. Its boiling-range allowance belongs to an isobaric path. Pause now to finish D four. If the fit does not converge, record no modeling verdict instead of guessing a result.

checks.title: Liquid stability · 100–105 min
checks.expected_narration: At fixed temperature and pressure, stable equilibrium is the admissible state with the lowest total Gibbs energy, subject to the material balance. For a binary mixture, the mixing-energy curve contains the ideal mixing terms plus the excess contribution. This curve can become nonconvex even when the activity model satisfies the Gibbs-Duhem identity exactly. That is why consistency does not imply a stable homogeneous liquid. Equality of chemical potentials identifies candidate coexisting phases. We must still ask whether that candidate provides the lowest energy when all allowed compositions are considered. In a binary plot, a globally supporting common tangent supplies that comparison. The line represents the energy of a mixture of the two endpoint liquids. Complete F one on page three: explain what remains to be checked after a solver has found equal chemical potentials. Pause briefly before continuing to the geometric condition.

Keep the original attempt so you can see what changed.
